query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In untreated Q235 steel, the native oxide film governs its corrosion behavior by providing effective protection under room‐temperature conditions but becoming compromised under high‐temperature (700–900 °C) salt exposure. Thermal stresses and salt‐driven reactions at high temperatures induce phase transformations and porosity (or even spallation) in the oxide film, thereby accelerating corrosion by exposing fresh metal.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its as-received, pre‐exposure state with a naturally formed native oxide film.
generation.intervention: Expose Q235 steel samples to controlled corrosive environments using a salt-containing medium at room temperature and at high temperatures (700–900 °C).
generation.conditions: This mechanism is expected to hold for untreated Q235 steel exposed to identical corrosive salts under conditions where thermal effects vary (ambient vs. high temperature). It applies when the native oxide film is unmodified and subject to standard exposure durations, but not if pre-treatments (e.g., annealing or engineered coatings) have altered the film.
generation.structural_mediator: The continuity, phase composition, and adhesion of the native iron oxide film mediate the extent of corrosion protection.
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, the stable oxide film acts as a barrier, limiting corrosion. Under high temperature, thermal energy and salt interactions induce rapid phase changes, increased porosity, and possible film spallation, which expose fresh metal and accelerate corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to room-temperature exposure, samples subjected to high-temperature salt environments will exhibit significantly higher mass change, observable degradation in the oxide film (increased porosity, phase shifts, or spallation), and reduced surface mechanical integrity.
generation.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel exposed to room-temperature salt conditions, which maintains a relatively intact oxide film and low corrosion rates.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is formulated for as-received Q235 steel with its native oxide film and may not extend to steels with engineered oxide layers or those that have undergone pre-treatments altering film properties.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative impact of the oxide film’s microstructural transformation on corrosion rate under high-temperature conditions remains uncertain and may depend on factors such as exposure duration and specific salt composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several batches of as-received Q235 steel samples. Expose one group to a room-temperature salt environment and another group to a high-temperature (700–900 °C) salt environment under identical exposure durations. Characterize the oxide film before and after exposure and quantify corrosion through mass change and mechanical property tests.
measurements: Mass change (to evaluate corrosion rate)
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for oxide film integrity (continuity, porosity, spallation)
X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase composition changes in the oxide film
Hardness or wear resistance tests as indicators of mechanical degradation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-temperature salt exposure does not result in a noticeably degraded oxide film (i.e., no significant increase in porosity, phase transformation, or spallation) and the corrosion rate does not significantly exceed that of the room-temperature baseline, then the proposed mechanism linking oxide film breakdown to accelerated corrosion would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: For Q235 steel in its as-received state, the nature of the native surface oxide film—its continuity, composition, and adherence—controls whether the steel retains corrosion protection or degrades under aggressive high‐temperature salt exposure. A dense, continuous oxide film acts as a barrier that slows corrosive attack, whereas a discontinuous or poorly adherent film allows localized salt-induced corrosion to propagate.
drafts.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its as-received condition, featuring a naturally formed native oxide layer acquired during storage and handling.
drafts.intervention: Compare specimens that retain their native oxide film with specimens from which the oxide film is selectively removed (e.g., by mild mechanical polishing or acid cleaning), with and without subsequent controlled thermal annealing.
drafts.conditions: Expose samples to aggressive salt environments at high temperatures (700–900 °C) and, in parallel, test under room-temperature conditions. Keep all other variables (exposure time, salt composition, atmosphere) constant to isolate the role of the initial oxide film.
drafts.structural_mediator: The continuity, phase composition, and adhesion of the native oxide layer (primarily iron oxides such as Fe2O3 and Fe3O4) serve as the mediator of protection.
drafts.mechanism: A continuous, well-adhered native oxide film acts as a physical barrier that retards the interfacial reaction between the corrosive salts and the steel substrate at high temperatures. Conversely, if the oxide film is discontinuous or compromised, localized salt attack accelerates corrosion by forming micro‐galvanic cells that enhance oxidation and mass loss.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature salt exposure, samples retaining the native oxide film (or enhanced via controlled annealing) will exhibit lower mass change, fewer surface defects, and better retention of hardness compared to oxide-removed specimens. At room temperature, the influence of the native oxide film is expected to be less pronounced.
drafts.baseline: The untreated Q235 steel in its as-received condition with its naturally formed oxide layer.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is expected to apply primarily to low-carbon steels like Q235 and may not extend to more highly alloyed or heat-treated steels. Additionally, the protective effect is anticipated in high-temperature salt environments and might not be significant under moderate or ambient conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples: one set retains the native oxide film and the other undergoes oxide removal (via controlled polishing and acid cleaning). Optionally, include a third set that is thermally annealed after oxide removal to examine any reformed oxide characteristics. Expose all sets to a controlled aggressive salt atmosphere at a fixed high temperature (e.g., 750 °C) for an identical duration, along with a similar test at room temperature as a control.
measurements: Mass change measurements (before and after exposure)
X-ray diffraction (XRD) and/or X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) for oxide phase and composition analysis
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for surface morphology and oxide scale continuity
Hardness testing to assess mechanical property retention
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the native oxide (or thermally enhanced oxide) do not exhibit statistically lower mass change, fewer surface defects, or improved hardness compared to the oxide-removed samples under high-temperature salt exposure, then the hypothesis that the native oxide film mediates corrosion protection is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In untreated (pre‐exposure) Q235 steel, the formation and stability of a native iron oxide scale governs its corrosion protection: at room temperature, microstructural features (such as a fine ferrite-pearlite distribution and inherent inclusions) promote the formation of a uniform, adherent passive oxide film that limits corrosion, whereas at high temperatures (700–900 °C) in the presence of aggressive salt environments, the same oxide scale undergoes rapid growth and phase transformations leading to scale spallation or porous, nonprotective structures that accelerate corrosion.
drafts.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its as-received, pre-exposure state with its native ferrite-pearlite microstructure and typical impurity inclusions.
drafts.intervention: Exposure of the steel to controlled corrosive environments: (1) a room-temperature aggressive electrolyte environment and (2) a high-temperature (700–900 °C) salt-containing environment.
drafts.conditions: The hypothesis applies under cyclic exposure conditions where thermal and chemical gradients are well controlled. It is expected to be valid for untreated Q235 steel, but would not apply if prior treatments (e.g., annealing or surface modifications) have altered the native oxide or microstructure.
drafts.structural_mediator: The integrity, composition, and adherence of the iron-based oxide scale (e.g., mixtures of Fe2O3 and Fe3O4) that forms spontaneously on the steel surface.
drafts.mechanism: Under room-temperature conditions, the native microstructure enables formation of a thin, uniform passive oxide film that protects the bulk metal. In contrast, at high temperatures in the presence of molten salt, accelerated oxidation kinetics and salt-induced chemical interactions lead to rapid thickening, phase changes, and spallation of this oxide layer, thereby undermining its protective function and resulting in increased corrosion.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline room-temperature exposure (or exposures without salt), samples exposed to high-temperature salt environments will display a significantly compromised oxide layer (e.g., increased porosity, spallation), higher mass change, and degraded mechanical properties. In contrast, room-temperature exposed samples should maintain a relatively intact, uniform oxide film and stable mass.
drafts.baseline: Q235 steel samples exposed to room-temperature corrosive conditions absent of aggressive high-temperature salt exposure.
drafts.boundary: This mechanistic hypothesis is expected to hold for untreated, as-received Q235 steel. It may not apply if the steel is pre-treated (e.g., annealed, surface-coated) to alter the native oxide scale or microstructure, or under corrosive environments where the salt chemistry does not interact with the oxide film in a disruptive manner.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Q235 steel samples in the as-received state. Expose one group to a controlled room-temperature corrosive environment and another group to a high-temperature (700–900 °C) salt-containing environment in a cyclic manner. Use identical exposure durations and cycles. Characterize the oxide layer structure via scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and measure mass change and hardness before and after exposure.
measurements: oxide layer thickness and continuity
phase composition and porosity of the oxide scale
mass change (indicative of oxidation rate)
microhardness and wear resistance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-temperature salt exposure does not result in a significantly disrupted oxide structure (e.g., similar thickness, phase composition, and integrity as observed at room temperature) or if the recorded mass change and mechanical degradation do not significantly differ from the room-temperature baseline, then the hypothesis that the native oxide scale’s behavior governs the switch from protection to degradation is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The naturally formed, thin iron oxide film on Q235 steel passivates the surface at room temperature but its integrity is compromised under high‐temperature salt exposure, where thermal stresses and salt-induced reactions cause film spallation, thereby exposing fresh metal that corrodes more rapidly.
drafts.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its as-received, pre-exposure condition featuring a naturally grown, thin oxide layer (predominantly Fe2O3/Fe3O4).
drafts.intervention: Expose samples to controlled environments: one set at room temperature (with a mild salt spray) and another at high temperature (700–900 °C) in an aggressive salt environment.
drafts.conditions: Comparisons are made between room-temperature exposure, where thermal stresses are minimal, and high-temperature conditions that impose significant thermal expansion and chemical reaction stresses on the oxide film. Testing should be conducted using identical salt compositions and exposure times.
drafts.structural_mediator: The integrity and adhesion of the native iron oxide film on the Q235 steel surface, which mediates the barrier to oxidation.
drafts.mechanism: At room temperature, the oxide film remains stable and adherent, effectively protecting the underlying metal. However, at high temperatures the mismatch in thermal expansion between the oxide layer and the metal, combined with salt-driven chemical interactions, leads to oxide film spallation. This breakdown exposes fresh metal to the corrosive environment and accelerates degradation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Q235 steel will exhibit minimal corrosion-related mass change and structural deterioration at room temperature due to the protective oxide film. In contrast, high-temperature salt exposure will result in significant mass loss, detectable film degradation (e.g., spallation or cracking), and increased corrosion rates relative to the room-temperature reference.
drafts.baseline: Q235 steel samples without salt exposure or maintained in an inert atmosphere; or samples exposed only to room-temperature conditions served as the reference state demonstrating effective protection by the intact oxide film.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is formulated for pre-exposed Q235 steel with its native oxide film and does not necessarily apply to steel that has undergone pre-treatment (such as engineered oxidation, alloying, or annealing) that modifies the oxide characteristics. It also may not be valid for materials with inherently stable, engineered oxide layers (like certain stainless steels or HEAs).

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple Q235 steel samples in their as-received condition. Divide samples between three groups: (1) Room-temperature exposure with a mild salt spray, (2) high-temperature (700–900 °C) exposure in the same aggressive salt environment, and (3) a control group maintained in an inert atmosphere. Monitor the evolution of the oxide film integrity and the mass change over time. Additionally, use a subset of samples with artificially thickened or mechanically enhanced oxide layers to assess the role of film adhesion.
measurements: Mass change over time (to quantify degradation rates).
Surface morphology and film integrity via SEM and optical microscopy.
Oxide phase identification using XRD and EDS.
Adhesion and spallation events monitored in situ if possible (e.g., with high-temperature environmental SEM).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-temperature salt exposure does not lead to a significantly greater mass change or visible oxide film degradation (i.e., spallation or cracks) compared to the room-temperature condition, or if the artificially thickened oxide layers do not show improved protection under high temperature, then the hypothesis that film spallation due to thermal stress is the governing mechanism for accelerated corrosion would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In Q235 steel as received, the native, thin, heterogeneous iron oxide film formed in ambient conditions initially provides limited corrosion protection at room temperature but transforms into a porous, non‐protective scale under aggressive high-temperature (700–900 °C) salt exposure. This phase transformation and microstructural degradation of the oxide film is the governing cause of accelerated corrosion at high temperatures, whereas its relative stability in room-temperature environments helps retain protection.
drafts.material_initial_state: Untreated Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state with the native atmospheric oxide film
drafts.intervention: Expose samples to controlled salt environments at room temperature and at 700–900 °C; additionally, compare samples that receive a preliminary annealing treatment (in an inert atmosphere) to stabilize/modify the oxide film versus those left in the native state.
drafts.conditions: The mechanism is expected to apply under aggressive salt exposure at high temperatures (700–900 °C), where thermal effects promote oxide phase transformation, but not at room temperature, where the native oxide film remains relatively intact.
drafts.structural_mediator: The microstructure and phase composition of the native iron oxide film (e.g., porosity, transition from protective oxides to less protective or porous phases) mediates the corrosion response.
drafts.mechanism: At room temperature, the native oxide layer acts as a modest barrier to corrosion. However, upon exposure to high-temperature salt environments, thermal energy induces phase changes and increases porosity in the oxide film; these changes compromise its protective function, leading to accelerated corrosion (as reflected in higher mass change and degradation of the steel substrate). In contrast, a pre-stabilized oxide film (via controlled annealing) is hypothesized to maintain a more homogeneous and protective structure at high temperatures, thus reducing corrosion.
drafts.predicted_outcome: At room temperature, Q235 steel will show minimal corrosion-related mass change. At high temperatures, untreated samples will display significant degradation (increased mass loss and oxide porosity and phase shifts) compared to the annealed samples, which should exhibit improved retention of the protective oxide phase.
drafts.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel subjected to room temperature salt exposure serves as the baseline condition with modest corrosion.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies to Q235 steel in its as-received, native oxide state and may not extend to alloyed or highly engineered steels (such as high-entropy alloys) that intentionally possess stabilized oxide layers.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples: one set in the untreated pre-exposure state and another set subjected to a controlled annealing process aimed at stabilizing the oxide film. Expose both sets to identical salt environments at room temperature and at 700–900 °C. Characterize the oxide film before and after exposure using SEM/EDS and XRD, and measure mass change and corrosion rates.
measurements: Mass change (corrosion rate)
X-ray diffraction patterns for phase identification
Scanning electron microscopy for oxide layer morphology
Optional electrochemical measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-temperature salt exposure does not lead to a detectable transformation (increased porosity, phase change) in the native oxide layer relative to the annealed samples, or if the corrosion rates at high temperatures are not significantly higher in untreated samples compared to annealed ones, the proposed mechanism linking oxide film transformation to accelerated corrosion would be falsified.
